result: This manuscript describes the Reproducibility Project: Cancer Biology, a collaboration between the Center for Open Science and Science Exchange that aims to replicate experiments from high-profile cancer biology papers published between 2010-2012, selected based on citations and Altmetric scores, with results to be published in eLife.
evaluation: Claims C1-C3 and C13-C14 describe the project structure, scope, and publication plans. These are straightforward descriptive statements about the project itself, supported by appropriate citations (C2, C3) and direct statements (C1, C13, C14). No experimental validation is required for these administrative/organizational claims.

result: Drug resistance in cancer arises through multiple mechanisms including intrinsic genetic alterations, acquired resistance during treatment, overexpression of efflux proteins, decreased drug uptake, alterations in drug targets, cell cycle checkpoint modifications, and therapy-induced selection of resistant subpopulations facilitated by tumor molecular heterogeneity.
evaluation: Claims C15-C23 present established background knowledge about cancer drug resistance mechanisms, all supported by appropriate citations to the literature. These are well-accepted concepts in cancer biology and serve as context for the study rather than novel findings.

result: NSCLC accounts for 85% of lung cancer cases in the developed world. EGFR activation promotes cell proliferation, migration, and survival, making it an attractive therapeutic target. While EGFR TKIs like gefitinib and erlotinib show initial clinical efficacy, most patients develop resistance, with mechanisms remaining unknown in up to 30% of cases.
evaluation: Claims C24-C32 provide established background on NSCLC epidemiology, EGFR biology, and clinical resistance patterns, all supported by appropriate literature citations. These represent accepted knowledge in the field rather than novel findings from this study.

result: Sharma and colleagues demonstrated that TKI exposure of PC9 cells (a TKI-sensitive NSCLC line) generates drug-tolerant persister (DTP) populations that are largely quiescent (G1 phase), acquire cancer stem cell markers (CD133, CD24), and can progress to proliferating expanded persisters (DTEPs) with prolonged exposure. This DTP phenotype has been confirmed by others and observed across multiple cancer types.
evaluation: Claims C33-C41 describe prior work by Sharma et al. and others, supported by citations and figure references. The reproducibility by independent groups (C36) and observation across cancer types (C37) strengthen confidence. These are established findings being replicated in this study, not new results.

result: DTPs generated by prolonged TKI exposure are reversible under drug-free conditions, with full restoration of TKI sensitivity, suggesting that acquired resistance may not require permanent genetic alterations and is not due to enhanced drug efflux mechanisms.
evaluation: Claims C4-C5 and C42-C44 describe the reversible nature of DTP drug tolerance from prior work (Sharma et al.), supported by figure citations. The inference that resistance may not require permanent genetic changes (C43) is reasonable given the reversibility data, though the word 'might' appropriately indicates this is interpretive. The exclusion of drug efflux (C44) provides mechanistic insight.

result: Epigenetic deregulation is common in cancer, involving DNA methylation and chromatin deacetylation. PC9 DTPs exhibit reduced histone 3 acetylation compared to parental cells, and treatment with the HDAC inhibitor trichostatin A (TSA) resensitizes DTPs to apoptosis.
evaluation: Claims C45-C47 provide established background on epigenetic mechanisms (supported by citations). Claims C48-C49 describe prior experimental findings from Sharma et al. with figure citations showing reduced H3 acetylation in DTPs and TSA-mediated resensitization. This connects epigenetic changes to the DTP phenotype.

result: HDAC inhibitors induce multiple anticancer effects including apoptosis, cell cycle arrest, differentiation, senescence, immune response modulation, and altered angiogenesis.
evaluation: Claims C50-C55 describe established biological effects of HDIs, supported by citation to Bolden et al. 2006. This is background knowledge providing context for why HDIs were tested in the study.

result: DTPs exhibited reduced histone acetylation and sensitivity to HDAC inhibitors. Testing of 13 pharmacological agents revealed that combined treatment of HDIs (TSA, SAHA, scriptaid, MS275) or IGF-1R inhibitor AEW541 with erlotinib prevented DTEP emergence. The synergistic TKI-HDI interaction has been confirmed in subsequent studies.
evaluation: Claims C6-C7 and C56-C59 describe prior findings from Sharma et al. showing that HDIs and IGF-1R inhibition prevent drug-tolerant colony formation when combined with TKIs. The synergistic interaction (C58) is supported by multiple subsequent studies, strengthening confidence. Figure citations support the experimental data.

result: Drug sensitivity was restored with co-treatment of either HDIs or IGF-1R inhibitor in combination with TKIs.
evaluation: Claims C8-C9 summarize the therapeutic finding from Sharma et al. that combining either HDIs or IGF-1R inhibitors with TKIs restores drug sensitivity, supported by figure citations. This represents a key finding about combination therapy approaches.

result: PC9 DTPs exhibit high basal expression of IGFBP3 (the high-affinity binding partner of IGF-I/II) and phosphorylated IGF-1R. IGF-1R inhibition completely abolished IGF-1R activation and significantly reduced expression of KDM5A, a histone demethylase that associates with histone deacetylases.
evaluation: Claims C60-C65 describe prior findings from Sharma et al. showing elevated IGF-1R pathway activity in DTPs and the effects of IGF-1R inhibition, supported by figure citations. The characterization of IGFBP3 (C61) and KDM5A (C65) as known proteins is appropriate background. The data connect IGF-1R signaling to epigenetic regulation.

result: Inhibition of IGF-1R activation led to decreased KDM5A expression and restoration of H3K4 methylation, suggesting a direct link between the IGF-1R signaling pathway and KDM5A function.
evaluation: Claims C10-C12 describe the mechanistic connection between IGF-1R signaling and epigenetic regulation through KDM5A from Sharma et al., supported by figure citations. The use of 'suggesting' (C12) appropriately indicates this is an interpretive conclusion from the data rather than direct demonstration of mechanism. The correlation between IGF-1R inhibition effects and KDM5A/H3K4 methylation changes supports the proposed link.

result: Murakami and colleagues demonstrated similar upregulation in IGF-1R activity in persistent TKI-selected NSCLC cells, though this phenotype was not attributed to chromatin modifications in their work.
evaluation: Claims C66-C67 describe independent confirmation of IGF-1R upregulation in drug-tolerant cells by Murakami et al., though with different mechanistic interpretation. This provides external validation of the IGF-1R finding while noting interpretive differences, which is appropriate scientific context.
